newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: E.Europe mkts mixed, investors turn to Prague.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe mkts mixed, investors turn to Prague.

text.p: Markets across central and eastern Europe were mixed this week, with key foreign investors turning their attention to Czech shares after recent strong gains in Hungary and Poland.
Bourses in Prague, Warsaw and Bratislava all gained ground, while Budapest dropped sharply on disappointing earnings reports and Croation shares eased. Romanian shares were mixed.
PRAGUE

Czech blue chip shares surged early in the week, as a spate of buying from abroad helped buoy a market which was otherwise quiet. The PX50 index closed on Thursday at 544.4, up 10.7 points from Monday's open.

Some analysts suggested that foreign investors may have decided to firm up their positions in the Czech Republic on the grounds that after strong gains in recent years in Poland and Hungary Prague was bound to be next.
"Fundamentally there's really no optimism...but after Hungary and Poland...some really believe that now is the time to go long into Czech paper," said Radim Bajgar of ING Barings.
WARSAW

Polish shares rose one percent to 16,920.4 points this week and analysts said that despite another likely profit-taking fall on Monday, enough stocks were attractively priced to return to growth by the middle of next week.
They said gains should not prove as large as during the recent six-session 14.5-percent surge led by large-cap banks but that rises by industrials could lead slower growth.

"Firms in the construction, power and furniture industries which are gaining from the recent flooding are a lot cheaper than comparable firms in Hungary or Russia," said Dariusz Piszczatowski of Polish Development Bank (PBR) house.
The bourse is closed on Friday for the Assumption holiday.
BUDAPEST

The Budapest bourse's fortunes turned sharply this week with the market sliding over seven percent, including an almost six percent plunge on Monday, as some first half earnings reports disappointed investors.
The dollar's weakening against the forint and losses on Wall Street also contributed to the market's downturn, and traders said the trend may continue in the next few days.

"The Dow weighs much (on the Budapest market) and if it continues to go down, we will probably go down, too," said Robert Stalmayer of AB-Moneta Kft. He added that the market's prospects remained optimistic for the longer term.
In central Europe, the Budapest bourse is most affected by movements on Wall Street due to its high proportion of foreign investors.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange continued to suffer through the dog days of summer this week, though slightly more action was seen on the part of foreign players.
The official 16-share SAX index closed at 170.56 Thursday, up 2.46 points from Monday's open.

"Most of the trading, for what it is, is from abroad because local players see more profits in the current domestic money market where rates are hovering at around 20 percent," Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt said.
"I don't remember such a dull period," Kruilt said, adding he saw no light at the end of the tunnel yet.
BUCHAREST
Bucharest stocks traded mixed this week in thin demand due to the summer holiday season.

Dealers said they do not expect a recovery until September, after new central bank regulations are introduced on the repatriation of profits, initial investments and capital gains for foreign investors.

On Thursday, three independent indices, based on average prices and market capitalisation, inched up by 0.2, 0.02 and 0.12 percent respectively from the previous day. Two were also slightly up on the week.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed lower across the board on Thursday after activity slowed down ahead of the long weekend which starts with a bank holiday on Friday.
Most blue chips suffered corrections with investor interest waning. One of the most liquid shares, drug maker Pliva, traded only 376 shares this week, compared to almost 17,000 last week.
Traders blamed the fall of prices and slower trading on a lack of investors, but disagreed over whether this pointed to a downward trend or was just a temporary correction.
LJUBLJANA
The Slovenian SBI index rose 1.49 percent this week to close on Thursday at 1,600.40.

"Many brokers feel better if they sell some of their shares before leaving on holiday. Most of the volume is usually accounted for by foreigners and they do not sell, so there was not much profit-taking," said Zoran Spasenic, a trader at brokerage BPH.
